hook.text: Nutrients float in soil water as charged particles called cations. If nothing holds them, rain washes them away.

buildup.text: Clay and humus particles carry negative charges on their surfaces—they attract and hold positive cations.

discovery.text: Cation exchange capacity (CEC) measures how many nutrients a soil can hold. Higher CEC means more fertile soil.

twist.text: Sandy soils have low CEC—nutrients wash out quickly. Clay soils hold nutrients but can also lock them up.

climax.text: Adding compost boosts CEC because organic matter provides those crucial negative charge sites.

punchline.text: CEC is your soil's ability to hold onto what plants need.

quiz.question: What does cation exchange capacity measure?
options: How many nutrient ions a soil can hold on its particles

details.summary: Cation exchange capacity (CEC) measures soil's ability to hold and release positively charged nutrient ions like calcium, magnesium, potassium, and ammonium. High CEC means soil can store more nutrients and resist leaching, making it a key indicator of fertility potential.
details.whyItMatters: CEC determines how much fertilizer a soil can hold before nutrients wash away. Sandy soils with low CEC need frequent small fertilizer doses, while clay soils with high CEC can store a season's worth of nutrients in one application.
takeaways: CEC measures soil's ability to hold positively charged nutrient ions on particle surfaces
Clay minerals and organic matter provide most of soil's cation exchange capacity
High CEC soils retain nutrients better and need less frequent fertilizer application

faq.question: What determines a soil's cation exchange capacity?
faq.answer: Clay particles and organic matter carry negative surface charges that attract and hold positively charged nutrient ions (cations). Soils with more clay and organic matter have higher CEC. Montmorillonite clay has very high CEC, while kaolinite and sand have low CEC.

faq.question: Why does CEC matter for fertilizer management?
faq.answer: Low CEC soils (sandy soils) cannot hold much fertilizer—nutrients leach quickly with rain. These soils need frequent, small fertilizer doses. High CEC soils (clayey soils) hold nutrients for months. CEC guides how much and how often to fertilize for maximum efficiency and minimum waste.
